walkthrough:
Link Location To Risk Of Blockage**
Respiratory bronchioles are the smallest bronchioles and they lead directly into alveoli. Their lumens are very narrow, so even a small amount of sticky mucus could easily block them and stop air reaching the alveoli for gas exchange.

Link Mucus To Slower Gas Exchange**
Gas exchange needs a very short diffusion distance. A layer of mucus over the wall would add extra distance for oxygen and carbon dioxide to diffuse across. There are also few or no cilia here to move mucus away, so it would stay and trap pathogens, increasing infection risk.
Final answer: Mucus would hinder/prevent airflow to alveoli as respiratory bronchioles are very narrow and close to alveoli. Mucus would increase the diffusion distance for oxygen and carbon dioxide.

walkthrough:
Bronchiole Epithelium For Protection And Cleaning**
The bronchiole in Fig. 4.1 shows a folded, thicker lining. Its cells are columnar to cuboidal in shape, so they are taller and thicker. Many are ciliated to help move mucus and trapped dust and pathogens upwards away from the lungs.

Alveolar Epithelium For Fast Diffusion**
Alveoli are surrounded by a very thin wall in the photo. Their epithelium is squamous, made of very flat thin cells forming a single layer. This gives a very short diffusion distance for oxygen into blood and carbon dioxide out of blood.

Make A Clear Paired Comparison**
So you state the difference directly: bronchiole - thicker columnar/cuboidal and ciliated, alveolus - thinner flat squamous and not ciliated. Do not mention goblet cells here because the question says other than goblet cells.
Final answer: Bronchioles have columnar/cuboidal ciliated epithelium with thicker/longer cells. Alveoli have squamous epithelium with thin/flat cells for short diffusion distance.

walkthrough:
Identify Tissue X**
Tissue X is the dark thin band surrounding the bronchiole. It is smooth muscle, which is involuntary muscle found in bronchiole walls. There is no cartilage in bronchioles to hold them open, so muscle is the main tissue controlling shape.

How Contraction Changes The Airway**
When smooth muscle contracts, it squeezes the wall and narrows the lumen diameter, constricting the bronchiole. When it relaxes, the lumen widens again. This is not the muscle of breathing itself, it only adjusts the airway size.

Why Control Airflow Matters**
Changing the diameter controls the resistance to airflow and therefore the volume of air reaching or leaving the alveoli supplied by that bronchiole. This allows distribution of air to match blood flow and demand.
Final answer: Tissue X = smooth muscle. It contracts/relaxes to decrease/change diameter of bronchiole/lumen to control volume/flow of air entering/leaving alveoli.
